options.text: Run Amazon Inspector on all EC2 instances in the main Region.
options.why: Inspector finds software vulnerabilities, not misuse of credentials, and the attack was in an unused Region.

options.text: Enable Amazon Detective in the management account.
options.why: Detective helps investigate findings after the fact; it needs a detection source like GuardDuty to start from.

questions.explain: GuardDuty is the managed threat detector; enable it organisation-wide through a delegated administrator with auto-enable, in every Region, including unused ones that attackers like.

questions.stem: A biobank stores sample metadata in Amazon RDS, Amazon EFS and DynamoDB. After a ransomware drill showed that an attacker with admin rights in the production account could delete both the resources and their backups, the biobank wants daily backups of all three services copied to a separate account in another Region, managed in one place. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Write a Lambda function for each service that creates daily snapshots and copies them to the other account and Region.
options.why: Works, but you build and maintain three backup tools, their schedules and their failure handling.

options.text: Enable RDS Multi-AZ, EFS replication and DynamoDB global tables into the other Region.
options.why: Replication copies deletions and corruption too, so a ransomware attack spreads to the replicas.

options.text: Turn on S3 Versioning for every bucket in the production account.
options.why: The data is in RDS, EFS and DynamoDB, not S3, and versions inside the compromised account can still be removed.

options.text: Create an AWS Backup plan covering the three services, with a copy rule to a backup vault in another account and Region.
options.why: One central policy for all three services, and the cross-account, cross-Region copy survives a compromised production account.

questions.explain: Backups must be isolated from the blast radius they protect against. AWS Backup centralises schedules across services and can copy to another account and Region; replication is not a backup.

questions.stem: Field ecologists in remote parts of South America, Africa and Southeast Asia upload 10-30 GB camera-trap archives to a single S3 bucket in eu-west-1. Uploads over long, lossy internet paths are slow and often fail. Each archive is uploaded once and processed in Europe. Which change MOST improves upload speed with the least effort?

options.text: Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration and upload through the accelerate endpoint with multipart upload.
options.why: Uploads enter the nearest AWS edge location and travel on the AWS backbone, and multipart upload retries only failed parts.

options.text: Create a bucket in each continent and replicate them to eu-west-1 with S3 Cross-Region Replication.
options.why: Shortens the first hop, but adds buckets, replication cost and per-site configuration, and the data still has to reach Europe.

options.text: Put an Amazon CloudFront distribution in front of the bucket and cache uploads at the edge.
options.why: CloudFront can forward PUT requests to the origin, but it does not cache uploads, and Transfer Acceleration is the simpler fit for large uploads to one bucket.

options.text: Order an AWS Direct Connect connection for each field site.
options.why: Direct Connect needs a physical link at a colocation facility; remote field camps cannot use it.

questions.explain: Large uploads from far-away clients to one bucket: Transfer Acceleration plus multipart upload. Many clients downloading the same content: CloudFront.

questions.stem: A dermatology startup hosts a small image-classification model on an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint backed by an always-on ml.m5.xlarge instance. The model runs on CPU and the endpoint gets a few hundred requests in short bursts during clinic hours and nothing overnight. The app tolerates an occasional extra second of latency. Which hosting option is MOST cost-effective?

options.text: Move the endpoint to a GPU instance so each request finishes faster.
options.why: Faster per request, but a GPU instance costs more per hour and still runs all night.

options.text: Use SageMaker AI batch transform jobs every 15 minutes.
options.why: Cheap for offline scoring, but clinicians need an answer per request, not every 15 minutes.

options.text: Deploy the model to a SageMaker AI serverless inference endpoint.
options.why: Serverless inference scales with traffic and bills per use, so idle hours cost nothing; occasional cold starts are acceptable here.

options.text: Keep the real-time endpoint and buy a SageMaker Savings Plan for it.
options.why: Cuts the hourly rate but still pays for an instance that is idle most of the day.

questions.explain: For intermittent inference traffic that tolerates cold starts, serverless inference avoids paying for idle instances. Real-time endpoints fit steady traffic; batch transform fits offline scoring.

questions.stem: A research hospital's 300 data scientists use Microsoft Entra ID for corporate sign-in. They need access to 25 AWS accounts with different roles per project, and leavers must lose AWS access the moment they are disabled in the corporate directory. Today each account has its own IAM users. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Keep IAM users but enforce MFA and a 90-day password policy in every account.
options.why: Hardens the users, but 25 separate user lists must still be cleaned up by hand when someone leaves.

options.text: Use AWS IAM Identity Center with Entra ID as the external identity provider, SCIM provisioning, and permission sets assigned per account.
options.why: Single sign-on from the corporate directory with automatic provisioning, so disabling a user there removes AWS access everywhere.

options.text: Create an Amazon Cognito user pool federated with Entra ID and give users IAM roles from an identity pool.
options.why: Cognito is for customer-facing app identity; using it for workforce console access across accounts is unsupported plumbing.

options.text: Set up a SAML 2.0 identity provider and roles separately in each of the 25 accounts.
options.why: Works without IAM users, but means 25 separate federations and role mappings to maintain.

questions.explain: Workforce access to many AWS accounts is IAM Identity Center connected to the corporate IdP, with SCIM for automatic provisioning and deprovisioning. Cognito is customer identity.

questions.stem: A medication-administration system sends dose events (ordered, given, cancelled) for each patient through an Amazon SQS standard queue. Occasionally a cancel is processed before the order it cancels, and some events are processed twice, causing wrong charts. Events for different patients do not need ordering relative to each other. Which change fixes this while keeping parallel processing?

options.text: Use one consumer thread for the existing standard queue so events are processed one at a time.
options.why: Standard queues still deliver out of order and occasionally twice, and a single consumer gives up all parallelism.

options.text: Switch to an SQS FIFO queue with the patient ID as the message group ID and a deduplication ID per event.
options.why: Ordering is kept within each patient's group, groups are processed in parallel, and deduplication removes duplicates within the dedup window.

options.text: Add a delay of 30 seconds to every message on the standard queue so earlier events arrive first.
options.why: Delays shift every message equally, so they do not create order and do nothing about duplicates.

options.text: Replace the queue with an SNS topic and an HTTPS subscription to the charting service.
options.why: SNS standard topics also give no ordering guarantee and can deliver more than once.

questions.explain: SQS FIFO orders messages per message group ID, so choose a group key (here the patient) that matches the ordering you need; distinct groups still process in parallel. Consumers should still be idempotent.

questions.stem: A multiplayer game sends gameplay events to an Amazon Kinesis data stream in provisioned mode with 20 shards, using the game's region code as the partition key. There are only five region codes. During a tournament producers receive `ProvisionedThroughputExceededException` while CloudWatch shows most shards nearly idle. Which actions resolve the throttling? (Choose two.)

options.text: Use a high-cardinality partition key, such as the player or match ID, so records spread across all shards.
options.why: With five keys, at most five shards receive data; a high-cardinality key spreads writes across every shard.

options.text: Append a random suffix (for example `EU#0`–`EU#9`) to the region code in the partition key and regroup by region in the consumers.
options.why: Spreading each region over ten key values lets its records land on many shards, removing the hot shards while keeping region-level grouping available downstream.

options.text: Switch the stream to on-demand capacity mode so Kinesis manages shard capacity as traffic grows.
options.why: Tempting because on-demand removes shard planning, but the per-shard write limit still applies and five region codes still hash to at most five shards, so the hot shards stay hot.

options.text: Double the shard count to 40 and keep the region code as the partition key.
options.why: Five keys still hash to at most five shards, so the extra shards stay idle and throttling continues.

options.text: Replace the producers' PutRecords calls with single-record PutRecord calls.
options.why: More calls with less batching increases overhead and does not relieve a hot shard.

questions.explain: Kinesis throughput limits are per shard, and the partition key's hash decides the shard. A low-cardinality key concentrates writes on a few shards no matter how many shards exist or which capacity mode is used; raise key cardinality (a natural high-cardinality id, or a salted key) before adding capacity.

questions.stem: A sleep-tracking app's backend is 80 Lambda functions written in Python that run about 2 billion invocations a month and make up most of the AWS bill. The functions use no native x86-only libraries. Which change will reduce the Lambda cost with the LEAST effort and no loss of performance?

options.text: Rewrite the functions as containers on Amazon EKS running on Spot Instance node groups.
options.why: Could be cheaper per hour, but it is a large migration and adds a cluster to run.

options.text: Raise every function's memory to 10 GB so they finish faster.
options.why: Higher memory can shorten runtime, but the price per millisecond rises much more than duration falls for most functions.

options.text: Buy EC2 Reserved Instances to cover the Lambda usage.
options.why: Reserved Instances apply to EC2 only; Lambda usage is covered by Compute Savings Plans, not RIs.

options.text: Change the functions' architecture to arm64 (Graviton) and redeploy after testing.
options.why: Lambda on arm64 has a lower price per GB-second and usually equal or better performance for portable code.

questions.explain: For portable Lambda code, switching to arm64 is a near-free price-performance gain. Also consider Compute Savings Plans, which cover Lambda, and right-sizing memory with measurements.

questions.stem: A gaming company serves its player portal at `play.example.com` through Amazon CloudFront, with its origin in eu-central-1. An engineer requested a public certificate from AWS Certificate Manager in eu-central-1, but it does not appear in the CloudFront distribution's certificate list. The company wants a free certificate that renews automatically. What should the solutions architect do?

options.text: Request a public ACM certificate for `play.example.com` in us-east-1 and attach it to the distribution.
options.why: CloudFront uses ACM certificates only from us-east-1; public ACM certificates are free and renew automatically.

options.text: Reissue the eu-central-1 certificate as exportable, export it, and upload it to IAM for CloudFront to use.
options.why: Exportable public certificates carry a fee and a certificate uploaded to IAM is not renewed automatically, so this misses both requirements.

options.text: Buy a certificate from a third-party authority and import it into ACM in eu-central-1.
options.why: Costs money, does not renew automatically, and imported into eu-central-1 it is still invisible to CloudFront.

options.text: Use the default `*.cloudfront.net` certificate and point a CNAME from `play.example.com` to the distribution.
options.why: Browsers would reject TLS for `play.example.com`, because the default certificate only covers the cloudfront.net domain.

questions.explain: CloudFront reads certificates from ACM in us-east-1 only; regional services such as ALB need the certificate in their own Region. Public ACM certificates are free and auto-renew.

questions.stem: A telemedicine booking app has an internet-facing Application Load Balancer, an application tier on EC2 in an Auto Scaling group, and an RDS database, all in private subnets except the load balancer. Instances are replaced often, so IP addresses change daily. The database must accept traffic only from the application tier. Which configuration is MOST secure and needs no updates when instances change?

options.text: A network ACL on the database subnets that allows port 5432 from the application subnets' CIDR ranges.
options.why: Works at subnet level, but any other resource placed in those subnets would also reach the database, and NACLs are stateless and harder to manage.

options.text: A database security group that allows port 5432 from the application tier's security group ID.
options.why: Rules that reference a security group follow instances as they come and go, and admit only members of that group.

options.text: A database security group that allows port 5432 from 0.0.0.0/0, because the database is already in a private subnet.
options.why: Private subnets are not a control by themselves; anything that can route to the subnet could connect.

options.text: A database security group that lists each application instance's private IP, updated by a Lambda function on scaling events.
options.why: Achieves the goal with fragile custom automation that can lag behind scaling events.

questions.explain: Chain security groups by reference (ALB SG to app SG to DB SG) so rules follow instances automatically. Use NACLs as a coarse, stateless subnet backstop, not as the main control.

questions.stem: A genomics research platform runs analysis containers in private subnets that reach the internet through NAT gateways. After a researcher's container sent data to an unknown host, security requires that outbound HTTPS be allowed only to an approved list of about 40 domains (package mirrors and partner APIs), centrally across 10 VPCs. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Restrict outbound rules in every security group to the current IP addresses of the 40 domains.
options.why: Domain IP addresses change often, especially behind CDNs, so the lists go stale and break or leak.

options.text: Use network ACLs on the private subnets to deny all outbound traffic except port 443.
options.why: Port 443 to any host is still allowed, so the leak that happened would still be possible.

options.text: Deploy AWS Network Firewall in an inspection VPC behind a Transit Gateway, with a stateful domain allow list for the approved domains.
options.why: Network Firewall can filter outbound HTTPS by domain name, and a central inspection VPC applies one policy to all 10 VPCs.

options.text: Enable Amazon GuardDuty to alert when containers contact unknown hosts.
options.why: GuardDuty detects suspicious activity after it happens; it does not block traffic.

questions.explain: Egress filtering by domain needs a layer-7-aware firewall such as AWS Network Firewall stateful domain lists; security groups and NACLs only understand IPs and ports. Centralise it with an inspection VPC and Transit Gateway.

questions.stem: A cloud-gaming company streams rendered game frames to players on 5G phones in several large cities. Even from the nearest AWS Region, round-trip latency is 30-40 ms, and the game needs single-digit milliseconds between the phone and the rendering server. Which solution meets the latency requirement?

options.text: Serve the stream through Amazon CloudFront from the nearest Region.
options.why: Edge caching helps static or repeatable content, but each player's frames are unique and rendered live, so there is nothing to cache.

options.text: Run the rendering servers in AWS Wavelength Zones in the carriers' 5G networks.
options.why: Wavelength places compute in the telecom provider's network, so 5G traffic reaches the server without leaving the carrier network.

options.text: Use AWS Global Accelerator in front of the rendering servers in the nearest Region.
options.why: Shortens the internet path to the Region, but the server is still in the Region, so latency stays well above single digits.

options.text: Place the rendering servers in a cluster placement group in the nearest Region.
options.why: Cuts latency between servers, not between the phone and the server.

questions.explain: When latency to mobile devices on 5G must be single-digit milliseconds, the compute has to move into the carrier network: Wavelength Zones. Local Zones and Outposts move compute near users or into your site; CloudFront and Global Accelerator only improve the path to a Region.

questions.stem: A stateless player-matchmaking API runs on 40 On-Demand instances at night and up to 200 during evening peaks, in an Auto Scaling group. The team must always keep at least 40 instances that cannot be interrupted, but can tolerate losing some extra capacity for a minute or two while it is replaced. Which configuration is MOST cost-effective?

options.text: Run all instances as Spot Instances of a single instance type to get the deepest discount.
options.why: Cheapest on paper, but one Spot pool can be reclaimed at once, breaking the 40-instance guaranteed floor.

options.text: Buy Reserved Instances for 200 instances to cover the peak.
options.why: Discounts the peak capacity, but pays for 160 instances that sit idle most of the day.

options.text: Use a mixed instances policy with an On-Demand base of 40 (covered by a Savings Plan) and Spot above the base, spread across several instance types.
options.why: The guaranteed floor stays On-Demand at a discounted rate, and the elastic peak runs on cheap Spot across diversified pools.

options.text: Keep all instances On-Demand and add scheduled scaling for the evening peak.
options.why: Scales well, but pays full On-Demand price for every peak instance.

questions.explain: Combine pricing models by layer: commitments (Savings Plans) for the steady floor, Spot across many instance types for the interruptible peak, On-Demand for anything in between.

questions.stem: A small team runs a containerised vaccination-record API on a single EC2 host with Docker Compose. The host has failed twice this year, and each time the team spent hours rebuilding it. The team has no Kubernetes experience and wants the API to survive an Availability Zone failure. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Run an Amazon ECS service on AWS Fargate with tasks in two or more AZs behind an Application Load Balancer.
options.why: No servers to manage, ECS replaces failed tasks, and tasks across zones behind the load balancer survive an AZ failure.

options.text: Create an Amazon EKS cluster with managed node groups across three Availability Zones and deploy the API with a Kubernetes Deployment.
options.why: Highly available, but it brings Kubernetes the team does not know, which is more operational overhead.

options.text: Keep Docker Compose and add a second EC2 host in another Availability Zone with Route 53 health checks.
options.why: Improves availability but leaves two hosts to patch and rebuild by hand, plus custom deploy scripts.

options.text: Take a nightly AMI of the host so it can be relaunched quickly.
options.why: Faster rebuilds, but the API is still down while someone notices and relaunches it.

questions.explain: For containers with the least ops, ECS on Fargate is the default; spread tasks across AZs behind a load balancer for availability. Choose EKS when you need Kubernetes itself.
